questions.stem: Sarah is a 30-year-old female who presents to her primary care physician with shortness of breath and chest pain on exertion. She reports feeling fatigued lately and has a family history of heart disease. On physical examination, her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, and her heart rate is 90 beats per minute. Auscultation of her heart reveals a harsh systolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border. An echocardiogram is ordered, which shows moderate aortic stenosis with a bicuspid aortic valve. What could be the most likely cause of Sarah's aortic stenosis?
questions.stemHtml: Sarah is a 30-year-old female who presents to her primary care physician with shortness of breath and chest pain on exertion. She reports feeling fatigued lately and has a family history of heart disease. On physical examination, her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, and her heart rate is 90 beats per minute. Auscultation of her heart reveals a harsh systolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border. An echocardiogram is ordered, which shows moderate aortic stenosis with a bicuspid aortic valve. What could be the most likely cause of Sarah's aortic stenosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Bicuspid valve calcification: A bicuspid aortic valve is a congenital cardiac defect in which the aortic valve has just two leaflets as opposed to three. The bicuspid aortic valve is a prevalent cause of aortic stenosis in young people. Exertional dyspnea, chest pain, exhaustion, and indicators of heart failure such as jugular venous distention and peripheral oedema are symptoms of aortic stenosis. A systolic ejection murmur is often heard best at the right upper sternal border during a physical examination. The diagnosis and degree of aortic stenosis are determined via an echocardiography. Currently, the most recommended treatment for moderate aortic stenosis is medical care to control symptoms. Surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement may be considered if aortic stenosis worsens or if medicinal therapy fails to adequately control symptoms. Incorrect Options: Option A - Rheumatic heart disease: Rheumatic heart disease occurs when untreated streptococcal infection damages the heart valves, generally in youth. Although rheumatic heart disease can cause aortic stenosis, it is a relatively uncommon cause in developed countries and is more commonly associated with mitral valve disease. The scenario's physical examination findings, including a harsh systolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border, are more consistent with aortic stenosis caused by a bicuspid aortic valve. A history of prior streptococcal infection is generally required to diagnose rheumatic heart diseas e, and blood tests such as the antistreptolysin-O (ASO) tit re may be needed to confirm the diagnosis. Antibiotics are often prescribed to treat the streptococcal infection underlying rheumatic heart disease, as well as drugs to control symptoms and prevent complications. In severe circumstances, valve repair or replacement may be essential. Option B - Age related aortic stenosis: Age-related aortic stenosis is a form of aortic stenosis caused by degeneration and calcification of the aortic valve in the elderly. This kind of aortic stenosis typically affects adults over the age of 65 and is more prevalent in males than in women . Senile degenerative aortic stenosis can produce dyspnea on exercise, chest pain, and weariness, but it is not the most common cause of aortic stenosis in a 30-year-old. The scenario's physical examination results, particularly a strong systolic murmur heard most prominently at the right upper sternal border, are more consistent with aortic stenosis induced by a bicuspid aortic valve. Medications are commonly used to treat senile degenerative aortic stenosis in order to manage symptoms and prevent consequences, such as heart failure and arrhythmias. In severe circumstances, it may be required to replace the valve. Option D - Congenital aortic stenosis: Congenital aortic stenosis, which can affect infants, children, and adolescents , is not the most prevalent cause of aortic stenosis in a 30-year-old. The scenario's physical examination results, particularly a strong systolic murmur heard most prominently at the right upper sternal border, are more consistent with aortic stenosis induced by a bicuspid aortic valve. The bicuspid aortic valve is a congenital heart anomaly in which the aortic valve has two leaflets instead of three and is a prevalent cause of aortic stenosis in young adults. Medication is often used to treat aortic stenosis caused by a bicuspid aortic valve in order to reduce symptoms and prevent consequences, such as heart failure or arrhythmias. In severe circumstances, it may be required to replace the valve. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient had 2 episodes of loss of consciousness in the past month and complains of occasional episodes of her heart ‘skipping a beat’. Past medical history is significant for treatment-resistant depression, hypertension and type II diabetes mellitus. ECG tracing is shown below. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 56-year-old female is admitted to the hospital due to palpitations and dyspnea. The patient had 2 episodes of loss of consciousness in the past month and complains of occasional episodes of her heart ‘skipping a beat’. Past medical history is significant for treatment-resistant depression, hypertension and type II diabetes mellitus. ECG tracing is shown below. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Amitriptyline: This patient’s clinical presentation and ECG findings suggest torsades de pointes . Long QT interval is the inciting factor that predisposes to torsades de pointes. ECG shows irregular QRS complexes of varying amplitude. This patient with treatment-resistant depression is most likely taking amitriptyline which causes the prolongation of QT interval. Other common causes of QT interval prolongation include: Antiarrhythmic (e.g. Class IA and IC) Antibiotics (e.g. macrolides) Antipsychotics (e.g. haloperidol) Antiemetics (e.g. ondansetron) Hypocalcemia Hypomagnesemia Hypokalemia Treatment options include: IV magnesium sulfate Atrial pacing IV isoprenaline Implantable defibrillator (QT > 500 msec) After the patient is stabilized, underlying causes should be rectified. Incorrect Options: Option A - Metformin: Option B - Lisinopril: Option D - Verapamil: Verapamil is used for rate control in patients with atrial fibrillation. Metformin is the oral drug of choice in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM) and works by inhibiting hepatic glucose production. Metformin doesn’t cause QT interval prolongation. Important side effects include: Vitamin B 12 deficiency Lactic acidosis Metformin should be used cautiously in patients with renal and hepatic dysfunction. Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACE inhibitor). It is commonly used as the drug of choice in patients with hypertension. Lisinopril doesn’t cause QT interval prolongation. Important side effects include: Hypotension Dry cough Angioedema Hyperkalemia Renal dysfunction Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker which usually affects the PR interval, so it would not cause QT interval prolongation. Common side effects include: Bradycardia Heart block Constipation Hypotension @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 37-year-old female immigrant from Guatemala presents to the emergency department complaining of fluttering in the chest that started 2 hours ago and has not improved. She reports losing weight of 15 pounds over the past 4 weeks. Her temperature is 98.7°F (37.0°C), blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, pulse 80/min, respirations 14/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On a physical exam, the patient's skin is hot and sweaty, with her eyes bulging out, and she appears irritated. An ECG is performed, revealing findings as seen in Figure. Which of the following is most likely the underlying cause of this patient's presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 37-year-old female immigrant from Guatemala presents to the emergency department complaining of fluttering in the chest that started 2 hours ago and has not improved. She reports losing weight of 15 pounds over the past 4 weeks. Her temperature is 98.7°F (37.0°C), blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, pulse 80/min, respirations 14/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On a physical exam, the patient's skin is hot and sweaty, with her eyes bulging out, and she appears irritated. An ECG is performed, revealing findings as seen in Figure. Which of the following is most likely the underlying cause of this patient's presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Decreased TSH: ECG demonstrates atrial fibrillation with a rapid and irregularly irregular rhythm with no discernible P-waves. The correct option is decreased TSH because this patient presents with chest pain and an ECG suggestive of atrial fibrillation. In the setting of her weight loss, protruding eyes and other symptoms of increased metabolism (such as sweating and anxiety), her atrial fibrillation is likely associated with hyperthyroidism (a decreased TSH). Atrial fibrillation typically presents with an odd sensation in the chest where the patient feels like their heart is racing. Typical causes include ischemic heart disease and connective tissue disorders ; however, hyperthyroidism is another potential cause of atrial fibrillation, and a decreased TSH level can support this diagnosis. Unstable patients should receive synchronized cardioversion. Stable patients can be given agents to slow their heart rate (such as calcium channel blockers and beta blockers). Incorrect Options: Option B - Dislodged thrombus: Pulmonary embolism is caused by dislodged thrombus which can present with chest pain, shortness of breath, and sinus tachycardia on ECG. This patient's ECG demonstrates an absence of P-waves suggesting a diagnosis of atrial fibrillation. ECG of patients with pulmonary embolism demonstrates a large S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III and an inverted T wave in lead III together indicate acute right heart strain. Option C - Ischemic heart disease: Ischemic heart disease presents with dull substernal chest pain and is associated with ST-elevation on ECG or a new left bundle branch block. Option D - Untreated anxiety: Untreated anxiety does not cause an absence of P-waves on ECG but could present with an odd sensation in the chest without any changes on ECG. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents in an outpatient clinic with complaints of intermittent palpitations and shortness of breath for the past several months. Past medical history is significant for asthma which is well-controlled. On examination, her physical examination is unremarkable. An electrocardiogram (ECG) is performed, and the patient becomes symptomatic during the recording. ECG is given below which is consistent with an Orthodromic AVRT. Her physician orders further testing to assess the structural and functional status of her heart and lungs. Ablation therapy is recommended but the patient is reluctant at the time. What medical therapy should be recommended to this patient?

Past medical history is significant for asthma which is well-controlled. On examination, her physical examination is unremarkable. An electrocardiogram (ECG) is performed, and the patient becomes symptomatic during the recording. ECG is given below which is consistent with an Orthodromic AVRT. Her physician orders further testing to assess the structural and functional status of her heart and lungs. Ablation therapy is recommended but the patient is reluctant at the time. What medical therapy should be recommended to this patient?

options.label: D
options.text: No therapy is required at this time

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Flecainide: This patient with an orthodromic AVRT secondary to WPW Syndrome should be placed on medical therapy until she is ready for any definitive treatment. The antiarrhythmic drugs of class IC flecainide and propafenone are the drugs of choice for preventing recurrent orthodromic AVRT. The presence of known coronary disease is an important exception, as class IC drugs can increase mortality due to proarrhythmic effects. Options such as Beta-blockers and Calcium channel blockers can be used to acutely terminate the arrhythmia but are not recommended for chronic therapy. Beta blockers are contraindicated in patients with asthma and hence a calcium channel blocker would be used for acute termination of this patient’s arrhythmia. WPW syndrome: It is an arrhythmia caused by an accessory electrical pathway that bypasses the AV node. The condition is usually congenital and can be associated with other cardiac defects. Orthodromic and Antidromic AVRT Antidromic and orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT) are two types of supraventricular tachycardia caused by an accessory pathway between the atria and ventricles. When an impulse travels down the normal atrioventricular (AV) node and back up through the accessory pathway, orthodromic AVRT occurs. With or without delta waves, the ECG shows a narrow QRS complex. However, antidromic AVRT occurs when an impulse travels down the accessory pathway and back up through the AV node. An ECG with or without delta waves shows a wide QRS complex. Symptoms: Most people with WPW syndrome are asymptomatic. Some experience a combination of these symptoms: palpitations, tachycardia, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, or syncope. Diagnosis: ECG: An accessory pathway allows electrical impulses to reach the ventricles more rapidly. Hence causing the characteristic: short PR interval widened QRS complexes, and delta waves. Once the diagnosis is confirmed, other tests are performed to assess the severity of the disease and heart function. Holter monitoring Electrophysiology study Echocardiography Treatment: Medical: Acute termination: Orthodromic AVRT: AV nodal blocking therapy via Vagal maneuvers or drugs such as Beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, Adenosine. Antidromic AVRT and Afib with preexcitation: Rhythm control with procainamide or ibutilide. The antiarrhythmic drugs of class IC flecainide and propafenone are the drugs of choice for preventing recurrent orthodromic and antidromic AVRT. The presence of known coronary disease is an important exception, as class IC drugs can increase mortality due to proarrhythmic effects. Catheter ablation: A procedure in which radiofrequency waves are used to destroy the accessory pathway. Surgical: In rare cases, surgery may be required to remove the accessory pathway. Complications: The most common complication of WPW syndrome is supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Other complications include atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation and heart failure. If left untreated, the arrhythmias from WPW syndrome can lead to hemodynamic instability, myocardial infarction and cardiac arrest. Incorrect Options: Option A & B - Propranolol & Carvedilol: Both of these are Beta blockers. Beta blockers can be recommended to control rate in patients with uncomplicated WPW Syndrome. They can also be used to acutely terminate or treat patients with orthodromic AVRT with low risk accessory tracts who are waiting for definitive management but are not 1st line therapy. Beta blockers are also contraindicated in patients with asthma as they can cause bronchoconstriction and exacerbate asthma symptoms Option D - No therapy is required at this time: If left untreated, WPW syndrome can lead to various arrhythmias which can ultimately culminate into hemodynamic instability, MI, cardiomyopathies, heart failure and sudden cardiac death. Therefore, it is important to have an early intervention. However, any medication should be used with caution and under direct supervision of a cardiologist @Neet_pg_bot

Option A & B - Propranolol & Carvedilol:

  • Both of these are Beta blockers.
  • Beta blockers can be recommended to control rate in patients with uncomplicated WPW Syndrome. They can also be used to acutely terminate or treat patients with orthodromic AVRT with low risk accessory tracts who are waiting for definitive management but are not 1st line therapy.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of recurrent chest pain, racing pulse, dizziness, and difficulty breathing. ECG recordings during episodes of tachycardia show a QRS duration of 100 ms, regular RR interval, and absent P waves. Which of the following is the likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of recurrent chest pain, racing pulse, dizziness, and difficulty breathing. ECG recordings during episodes of tachycardia show a QRS duration of 100 ms, regular RR interval, and absent P waves. Which of the following is the likely underlying cause of this patient's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Macroreentrant rhythm in the right atrium through the cavotricuspid isthmus

options.label: C
options.text: Fibrosis of the sinoatrial node and surrounding myocardium

options.label: D
options.text: AV node with slow and fast pathway

questions.answerText: AV node with slow and fast pathway
questions.solution: Correct Option D- AV node with slow and fast pathway: This patient most likely suffers from paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) , most commonly caused by atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT). AVNRT is a tachyarrhythmia caused by a dysfunctional AV node with two electrical pathways, one fast with a long refractory period and one slow with a short refractory period (dual AV nodal physiology). During normal sinus rhythm, the conduction occurs via the fast pathway, and the incoming current from the slow pathway is extinguished. Typical AVNRT is triggered by an atrial premature beat (APB). An APB arrives at the AV node during the fast pathway's refractory period. The impulse is, therefore, conducted through the slow pathway, which is out of its refractory period. When the impulse reaches the distal junction of the two pathways, the fast pathway has recovered its excitability, and the impulse can travel retrograde. The impulse reaches the atria, leading to an almost simultaneous depolarization of the atria and ventricles. The current reenters the slow pathway. A reentry circuit is created with anterograde conduction across the slow-conducting pathway and retrograde conduction in the fast pathway resulting in sustained tachycardia. Alternative electrical conduction pathways (one fast and one slow) in the atrioventricular node (AV node) are the underlying cause of AVNRT. questions.solution: Correct Option C- Chronic alcohol abuse: A known risk factor for the onset of myocarditis is chronic alcohol usage. Alcohol can have toxic effects on the heart muscle, which can result in inflammation and cell damage. Chronic alcohol misuse can also impair immunity, leaving the body more vulnerable to illnesses resulting in myocarditis. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hypertension: A chronic illness known as hypertension causes higher arterial blood pressure. Option B- Hyperlipidemia: Although hyperlipidemia is not a known risk factor for myocarditis, it is a risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Option D- Diabetes Mellitus: A chronic metabolic condition called diabetes mellitus is characterized by elevated blood sugar levels. Diabetes is an established risk factor for coronary artery disease and heart failure, among other cardiovascular disorders, but it is not one for myocarditis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male farmer presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset palpitations and a strange sensation in his chest while working in the field. He has never seen a physician and has a history of regular alcohol consumption and pipe smoking. Her temperature is 98.7°F (37.0°C), blood pressure 78/54 mmHg, pulse 148/min, respiration is 22/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. An ECG is performed, which is shown in Figure. What is the best initial step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old male farmer presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset palpitations and a strange sensation in his chest while working in the field. He has never seen a physician and has a history of regular alcohol consumption and pipe smoking. Her temperature is 98.7°F (37.0°C), blood pressure 78/54 mmHg, pulse 148/min, respiration is 22/min, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. An ECG is performed, which is shown in Figure. What is the best initial step in management?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Synchronized cardioversion: This patient presents with unstable vitals signs and an ECG suggestive of atrial fibrillation . The best initial step in management is synchronized cardioversion. Atrial fibrillation is a medical condition characterized by an irregular and often rapid heartbeat. Patients with this condition typically experience an unusual sensation in their chest and may notice that their heart is beating faster than usual. This condition often occurs in patients with a history of ischemic heart disease, valvular abnormalities, or connective tissue disorders. In some cases, patients with atrial fibrillation may become unstable due to a rapid heart rate and low blood pressure. These patients require immediate cardioversion, a procedure that uses an electrical shock to restore a normal heart rhythm. A form of electrical cardioversion in which a low-energy shock is delivered at or just after the peak of the R-wave of the QRS complex. Synchronized electrical cardioversion is indicated in almost all unstable patients with tachycardia and a pulse. Incorrect Options: Option A- Adenosine: Adenosine is used to treat supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), a different type of arrhythmia. The patient's ECG shows atrial fibrillation, which is not a form of SVT and is not responsive to adenosine. Adenosine is typically used to treat SVT when vagal manoeuvres are ineffective or when the patient is symptomatic or hemodynamically unstable. It works by slowing conduction through the AV node and interrupting the re-entry pathway responsible for SVT. Adenosine has a short half-life and is rapidly metabolized, making it an ideal agent for the acute termination of SVT. It is administered as a rapid IV push followed by a saline flush, and patients may experience a brief period of asystole or bradycardia before the sinus rhythm is restored. Option B- Diltiazem: Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker used to slow the heart rate and treat atrial fibrillation in hemodynamically stable patients. However, in this case, the patient is hemodynamically unstable with low blood pressure and a rapid heart rate. This requires immediate intervention to restore a normal rhythm and prevent further complications. Option C- Metoprolol: It is a beta-blocker and is an initial treatment of choice for atrial fibrillation in stable patients. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: The Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic congenital heart disease. Which of the following is a clinical feature of this condition?
questions.stemHtml: The Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic congenital heart disease. Which of the following is a clinical feature of this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Notching of the inferior rib borders

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Ventricular septal defect: The infundibular septum separates the pulmonary and aortic outflows. During cardiac development, its anterior deviation results in a cyanotic heart condition, the Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), characterised by four abnormalities. Pulmonary stenosis leading to right ventricular outflow obstruction. The aorta overrides the ventricular septum due to its dextroposition. Ventricular septal defect Hypertrophy of the right ventricle (RV) Due to pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular contraction shunts blood to the left ventricle, although the right atrial and ventricle venous return is normal. Consistent desaturation of the blood results in cyanosis. A narrow heart base and left heart border concavity occupy the area normally occupied by the pulmonary artery, as found on the anteroposterior chest x-ray. RV is hypertrophied and points horizontally to the chest wall, and the apical shadow is uptilted. It is situated above the diaphragm higher than normal, and the cardiac silhouette appears on the X-ray like a boot. Symptoms like right ventricular hypertrophy and cyanosis severity depend on the degree of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Incorrect Options: Option A- Notching of the inferior rib borders: Inferior rib borders’ notching is characteristic of coarctation of the aorta in which collateral vessels supply blood to the descending aorta. Pressure erosion of the ribs by these vessels results in the notching of the ribs. Complaint of pain in both legs after exercise is common, and radio-femoral delay is present on examination. Pulses in the lower extremities are weak, whereas bounding in the upper extremities and carotid artery are seen. It is not associated with TOF. Option B- Atrialization of the right ventricle: Right ventricle’s atrialization occurs in Ebstein anomaly , a condition in which the tricuspid valve is abnormally displaced downwards into the right ventricle. All valve leaflets adhere to the right ventricular wall apart from the anterior cusp. Enlargement of the right atrium occurs due to tricuspid valve regurgitation. A holo-systolic murmur can be heard over most of the left anterior chest. Broad normal or tall P-waves and right bundle branch blocks are common ECG findings. It is not associated with TOF. Option D- Total anomalous pulmonary venous return: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return has no direct connection between the pulmonary veins and the left atrium. They may drain directly into the superior vena cava by a vertical vein, right atrium, or descending vein into the inferior vena cava. There is a mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood at the right atrium. Right ventricular hypertrophy is a common ECG finding. Surgery should be performed for the correction of the abnormality. It is not associated with TOF. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: An 80-year-old male smoker was diagnosed with an aortic aneurysm. He is a known case of Marfan syndrome. On USG, the size of the aortic aneurysm is 4 cm, and the patient is asymptomatic. Which of the following is the indication for surgery in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: An 80-year-old male smoker was diagnosed with an aortic aneurysm. He is a known case of Marfan syndrome. On USG, the size of the aortic aneurysm is 4 cm, and the patient is asymptomatic. Which of the following is the indication for surgery in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Distal embolisation: Patients with an aortic aneurysm less than 5.5cm and no associated symptoms should undergo surgical repair if there is distal embolization. Distal embolization is the strongest indication of surgical repair irrespective of the size of the aneurysm because if not repaired, it will lead to limb loss. Thrombus can form within the aneurysmal sac, and sometimes it can dislodge. The dislodged thrombus then acts as an embolic source of ischemia in the lower limbs, resulting in acute limb ischemia that can lead to loss. Incorrect Options: Option A- Marfan syndrome: Marfan syndrome is associated with a thoracic aortic aneurysm. Asymptomatic and small aortic aneurysms associated with Marfan syndrome do not indicate surgical repair. Option B- Size of the aneurysm: The patient has an aortic aneurysm which is 4cm in size. Suppose a patient has an aortic aneurysm that is less than 5.5 cm and is asymptomatic. In that case, surgery is unnecessary because the risk outweighs the risk of rupture until the abdominal aortic aneurysm reaches the maximum size of 5.5cm. Option D- Pain: This patient is asymptomatic and has no pain, so it is not an indication of surgical repair in this patient. All symptomatic patients should be considered for surgical repair as it will not relieve the symptoms but decrease the risk of rupture as pain predates rupture. @Neet_pg_bot

Currently, the patient is vitally stable and doesn’t complain of any chest pain or shortness of breath. His pulse rate is 50 bpm, and his blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg. An ECG strip of the patient is shown below. Which of the following is the definitive treatment option for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. Past medical history is significant for hypertension, myocardial infarction, and asthma. Currently, the patient is vitally stable and doesn’t complain of any chest pain or shortness of breath. His pulse rate is 50 bpm, and his blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg. An ECG strip of the patient is shown below. Which of the following is the definitive treatment option for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Permanent pacemaker: The ECG findings of this patient are consistent with a third-degree heart block, also called a complete heart block. In the third-degree heart block, there is a complete failure of conduction and atria, and the ventricle contracts independently. Ventricular rhythm is maintained by one of the following: AV node Bundle of His Distal Purkinje tissue The heart cannot compensate, and there is a fall in the stroke volume. Syncope , without any preceding symptoms, is a common clinical presentation. Patients with asystole can be temporarily managed with IV atropine or isoprenaline. Permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for third-degree heart block. Prognosis is good after the placement of the pacemaker. A permanent pacemaker is also indicated for Mobitz type II second-degree heart block because of an increased risk of sudden cardiac death. Incorrect Options: Option A- Propranolol: Propranolol is a non-selective β-blocker that belongs to the class II antiarrhythmic and reduces the rate of SA node depolarization and increases the PR interval without any effect on ERP. It doesn’t play any role in managing complete heart block. It also slows the AV node’s conduction, making it suitable for rate control in patients with atrial flutter or fibrillation. Propranolol is contraindicated in patients with asthma because it causes bronchospasm. Other side effects include: Myocardial depression Bradycardia Impotence Fatigue Depression Option B- Adenosine: Adenosine is a first-line agent in managing supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). The three main types of SVT are: Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia Atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia Atrial tachycardia SVTs are a narrow complex tachycardias. Adenosine binds to the A1 receptors in the conducting tissue. It decreases AV node conduction by hyperpolarization of the cell. Common side effects include: Flushing Hypotension Bronchospasm Chest pain It is contraindicated in patients with asthma. Option D- Cardiac resynchronization therapy: Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) is done in selected patients with left ventricular systolic dysfunction secondary to the left bundle branch block . Following systems are used to deliver CRT: Right atrial lead. Right ventricular lead. A lead placed into the left ventricle epicardial vein. CRT improves mortality in patients with heart failure (NYHA class III-IV) having an ejection fraction of <35%. CRT pacemakers are also used in palliative treatment. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old patient with a history of hypercholesterolemia presents to the clinic for a follow-up visit. The patient is currently taking atorvastatin for lipid control. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of atorvastatin?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old patient with a history of hypercholesterolemia presents to the clinic for a follow-up visit. The patient is currently taking atorvastatin for lipid control. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of atorvastatin?

options.label: A
options.text: Inhibition of lipolysis in adipose tissue

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase: Statins include atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin, pravastatin, and lovastatin. Mechanism of action of statins: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase , an enzyme that catalyses the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, which is a precursor for cholesterol synthesis. By inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, statins reduce the production of cholesterol in the liver and increase the uptake of LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream by the liver. This results in a decrease in serum LDL cholesterol levels. Uses of statins: Hypercholesterolemia (LDL cholesterol >190 mg/dl) Coronary artery disease Stroke Peripheral artery disease Side effects of statins: Gastrointestinal disturbance Hepatotoxicity Myalgia Myopathy Rhabdomyolysis Incorrect Options: Option A- Inhibition of lipolysis in adipose tissue: Niacin works by inhibiting hormone-sensitive lipase, an enzyme involved in the breakdown of triglycerides in adipose tissue. By inhibiting this enzyme, niacin decreases the release of free fatty acids from adipose tissue, which reduces the liver's synthesis of VLDL and ultimately lowers the level of LDL cholesterol in the bloodstream. Side effects of niacin include flushing, itching, hyperuricemia and hepatotoxicity . Option B- Activation of PPAR-alpha receptors: Fibrates work by activating peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR-alpha), a transcription factor involved in regulating lipid metabolism. By activating this receptor, fibrates increase lipoprotein lipase expression , which is involved in the degradation of LDL and triglycerides. Fibrates are used to treat hypertriglyceridemia. Side effects of fibrates include myopathy, hepatotoxicity, and cholelithiasis. Option D- Inhibition of intestinal cholesterol absorption: Ezetimibe works by inhibiting the Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 (NPC1L1) protein, which is responsible for the intestinal absorption of cholesterol. By inhibiting this protein, ezetimibe reduces cholesterol absorption from the diet, ultimately lowering the level of LDL cholesterol in the bloodstream. Ezetimibe is used to treat hypercholesterolemia Side effects of ezetimibe include myalgia, diarrhoea, and elevated liver enzymes @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 70-year-old female presents to the ER complaining of the “worst headache of my life.” Vital signs are T 98°F, HR 109, BP 225/103, RR 22, and SpO2 96% on room air. A hemorrhagic stroke is suspected. Which of the following is true regarding hemorrhagic stroke care?
questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old female presents to the ER complaining of the “worst headache of my life.” Vital signs are T 98°F, HR 109, BP 225/103, RR 22, and SpO2 96% on room air. A hemorrhagic stroke is suspected. Which of the following is true regarding hemorrhagic stroke care?

options.label: A
options.text: Aggressive blood pressure lowering may help prevent hematoma expansion.

options.label: B
options.text: Prophylactic anticonvulsants are recommended for all patients.

options.label: C
options.text: Carotid endarterectomy is indicated for surgical treatment of hemorrhagic stroke.

options.label: D
options.text: Tissue plasminogen activator is standard treatment for hemorrhagic stroke.

questions.answerText: Aggressive blood pressure lowering may help prevent hematoma expansion.
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Aggressive blood pressure lowering may help prevent hematoma expansion: Hypertensive patients with spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) should be managed with antihypertensives to lower blood pressure in order to prevent hematoma expansion and rebuilding. For patients with acute ICH who present with systolic blood pressure between 150 and 220 mmHg, it is generally recommended that the SBP be lowered to 140 mmHg. For patients with an SBP >220 mmHg, a more aggressive reduction of blood pressure is indicated. Most experts recommend a target SBP of 140 to 160 mmHg. Because this patient's systolic blood pressure is >220 mmHg, a continuous IV infusion of antihypertensives (versus intermittent IV bolus) is indicated. While hemorrhaging stroke increases the risk for seizures, prophylactic anticonvulsants are not indicated for all patients but may be considered in some with unsecured aneurysms and large concentrations of blood at the cortex. Seizures should be treated promptly. Incorrect Options: Option B - Prophylactic anticonvulsants are recommended for all patients: Prophylactic anticonvulsants are not recommended for all patients with hemorrhagic stroke. While it is true that hemorrhagic strokes can increase the risk of seizures, giving prophylactic anticonvulsants to all patients is not supported by strong evidence and may even lead to worse neurologic and cognitive outcomes in some cases. The decision to use prophylactic anticonvulsants should be individualized and considered on a case-by-case basis. They may be considered in patients with certain risk factors, such as unsecured aneurysms or large concentrations of blood at the cortex, where the risk of seizures is higher. Option C - Carotid endarterectomy is indicated for surgical treatment of hemorrhagic stroke: Carotid endarterectomy is not indicated for the surgical treatment of hemorrhagic stroke. Carotid endarterectomy is a surgical procedure used to treat ischemic stroke caused by carotid artery stenosis, where plaque buildup in the carotid artery restricts blood flow to the brain. It is not a treatment for hemorrhagic stroke, which involves bleeding within the brain parenchyma due to the rupture of blood vessels. Option D - Tissue plasminogen activator is standard treatment for hemorrhagic stroke: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is not the standard treatment for hemorrhagic stroke. tPA is a thrombolytic agent used for the treatment of ischemic stroke caused by a blood clot blocking a blood vessel in the brain. In hemorrhagic stroke, there is bleeding within the brain, and the use of tPA would not be appropriate as it could worsen the bleeding. tPA is contraindicated in hemorrhagic stroke and should only be used in ischemic stroke when specific criteria are met. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 44-year-old female with suspected myasthenia gravis is planned for robotic thymectomy under general anesthesia. During the preoperative anesthesia evaluation, he related a history of recurrent pulmonary aspiration and significant ocular weakness. Which of the following antibodies are likely to be present in the plasma and can be used for preoperative screening of myasthenia gravis?
questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old female with suspected myasthenia gravis is planned for robotic thymectomy under general anesthesia. During the preoperative anesthesia evaluation, he related a history of recurrent pulmonary aspiration and significant ocular weakness. Which of the following antibodies are likely to be present in the plasma and can be used for preoperative screening of myasthenia gravis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Anti-muscle-specific kinase antibodies: Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor antibodies are the most common antibodies found in patients with myasthenia gravis. These antibodies are present in nearly 95% of patients diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. Other groups of patients with significantly higher involvement of bulbar muscles have muscle-specific kinase antibodies. These antibodies occur in nearly 50% of patients with myasthenia gravis. They are produced against the phosphorylating enzyme in the skeletal muscles. Their role is defined in patients with bulbar involvement or in patients seronegative for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. The sensitivity is in the following order: acetylcholine receptor (postsynaptic) > muscle-specific kinase antibodies. Incorrect Options: Option A - Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies (pre-synaptic): Unlike Lambert-Eaton syndrome where the antibodies are against presynaptic calcium channels, myasthenia is primarily a postsynaptic disorder. Antibodies are produced against postsynaptic receptors or muscle-specific kinase. This describes the presynaptic antibody, which is not related to myasthenia. Option B - Anti-acetylcholinesterase antibodies: Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme that metabolizes the acetylcholine released in the synaptic cleft. Destruction of this enzyme would produce symptoms similar to organophosphate poisoning. This would lead to increased activity of both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Myasthenia is primarily a disease of nicotinic receptors, and these antibodies have no relation to myasthenia gravis. Option D - Anti-thymocyte globulin antibodies: Patients with thymoma have a high incidence of myasthenia gravis. This has been attributed to a T-cell-mediated autoimmune response observed in patients with hyperactive thymus. This, however, is not related to anti-thymocyte globulin antibodies. These antibodies are therapeutically used in patients who receive transplanted organs and are used for immunosuppression. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A first-time mother presents with her 9-day-old infant who has experienced seizures. The infant had an uncomplicated term delivery and has been otherwise well. The infant has been and remains afebrile. The mother reports diluting the baby's formula. What is the most likely cause of this infant's seizures?
questions.stemHtml: A first-time mother presents with her 9-day-old infant who has experienced seizures. The infant had an uncomplicated term delivery and has been otherwise well. The infant has been and remains afebrile. The mother reports diluting the baby's formula. What is the most likely cause of this infant's seizures?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hyponatremia: In a well newborn without a fever, hyponatremia is the most common cause of seizures. Water intoxication is the most common cause of hyponatremia during infancy. Infants are unable to concentrate urine adequately, so parents who dilute formula or give their infants tap water put their infants at risk. Other causes of neonatal seizures also include neonatal encephalopathy and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, structural brain injuries, including ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke; glucose or other electrolyte abnormalities; and systemic or CNS infections. In a well-baby, a genetic epilepsy syndrome such as benign familial neonatal epilepsy may be the cause. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hypokalemia: Hypokalemia is uncommon in infancy and does not typically cause seizures. Option C - Hypocalcemia: Hypocalcemia is also a common cause of seizures in neonates, so serum calcium levels should be checked. In fact, all infants have a slight decline in serum calcium levels with a nadir at 24 to 48 hours. Symptomatic hypocalcemia is more common in infants of diabetic mothers, preterm infants, or infants with a history of anoxic encephalopathy. Option D - Hypomagnesemia: Hypomagnesemia is not as common as hypocalcemia, but symptoms of hypomagnesemia mimic those of hypocalcemia. It is difficult to correct hypocalcemia if the serum magnesium is also low. Therefore, infants with seizures should have a comprehensive evaluation of their electrolytes. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Differences between Aδ fibers and C nociceptive fibers include all of the following, EXCEPT?
questions.stemHtml: Differences between Aδ fibers and C nociceptive fibers include all of the following, EXCEPT?

options.label: A
options.text: Aδ fibers have a larger diameter than C fibers

options.label: B
options.text: C fibers conduct slower than Aδ fibers

options.label: C
options.text: Aδ fibers are high threshold mechanoreceptors whereas C fibers are low threshold polymodal (i.e., respond to all forms of noxious stimuli) receptors

options.label: D
options.text: Local anesthetics are more likely to work on Aδ fibers rather than C fibers

questions.answerText: Local anesthetics are more likely to work on Aδ fibers rather than C fibers
questions.solution: that the statement has Aδ and C fibers reversed. Local anesthetics block C fiber transmission whereas applied pressure can block Aδ fibers. Aδ fibers are larger, more heavily myelinated, and faster conducting than C fibers. Aδ nociceptors are higher threshold mechanoreceptors that respond to noxious mechanical stimuli (e.g., sharp objects) and some also serve as mechanothermal nociceptors and will respond to noxious thermal stimuli. C nociceptors respond nonselectively to all forms (thermal, mechanical, noxious) of noxious stimuli but conduct slower than Aδ fibers resulting in the concepts of “first” and “second” pain. When an injury occurs there is a first wave of brief, sharp pain transmitted by Aδ fibers followed by a second wave of more prolonged and distressing pain, often with a burning quality, transmitted by C fibers. The difference in conduction velocities (for the reasons listed above) between these two fiber types is responsible for this difference in “first” and “second” pain. Incorrect Options: Option A - Aδ fibers have a larger diameter than C fibers: This statement is true. Aδ fibers are myelinated and have a larger diameter compared to C fibers, which are unmyelinated. The myelination of Aδ fibers allows them to conduct nerve impulses faster than C fibers. Option B - C fibers conduct slower than Aδ fibers: This statement is true. Aδ fibers are fast-conducting nerve fibers, transmitting sharp, well-localized pain signals rapidly. In contrast, C fibers are slow-conducting fibers, responsible for the transmission of dull, poorly localized, and aching pain signals. Option C - Aδ fibers are high threshold mechanoreceptors whereas C fibers are low threshold polymodal (i.e., respond to all forms of noxious stimuli) receptors: This statement is true. Aδ fibers are sensitive to mechanical stimuli and respond to high-threshold mechanical inputs, such as strong pressure and noxious mechanical stimuli. They are responsible for the initial sharp pain experienced when, for example, you pinch your finger. On the other hand, C fibers are polymodal nociceptors that respond to various noxious stimuli, including mechanical, thermal, and chemical stimuli. They are responsible for the prolonged, burning, and aching pain experienced after the initial sharp pain. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Spasticity, a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone, is a complication of many neurological disorders affecting the brain and/or spinal cord. Baclofen is often used to alleviate spasticity symptoms in neurological disease. Which of the following options best describes its mechanism of action?
questions.stemHtml: Spasticity, a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone, is a complication of many neurological disorders affecting the brain and/or spinal cord. Baclofen is often used to alleviate spasticity symptoms in neurological disease. Which of the following options best describes its mechanism of action?

options.label: A
options.text: Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that reduces the release of excitatory neurotransmitters

options.label: D
options.text: Blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle cells

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-B receptor agonist: Baclofen is often used to treat spasticity in neurological disease. It works as a gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-B receptor agonist that acts at the level of the spinal cord and supraspinal sites. It can be given orally or intrathecally via a baclofen pump. Side effects include sedation and weakness. It cannot be discontinued abruptly because of serious withdrawal symptoms that can include seizures and hallucinations. Incorrect Options: Option A - Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that reduces the release of excitatory neurotransmitters: Tizanidine works as an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that reduces the release of excitatory neurotransmitters. Option C - Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-A receptor agonist: Benzodiazepines enhance the effect of the GABA-benzodiazepine complex through the agonist effects at the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-A receptor. Option D - Blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle cells: Dantrolene, a peripherally acting muscle relaxant, blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum directly in skeletal muscle cells. Option E - Central-acting skeletal muscle relaxant pharmacologically similar to tricyclic antidepressants: Cyclobenzaprine is a central-acting skeletal muscle relaxant pharmacologically similar to tricyclic antidepressants. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia wakes with left-sided weakness affecting his face, arm, and leg, double vision, and profound ataxia. His wife quickly calls an ambulance and arrives at the emergency room one hour after waking from sleep. On further questioning, you determine his last known well time to be 10 p.m. the night prior (9 hours prior to the presentation). His NIHSS is 6. A non-contrast CT shows no intracranial hemorrhage and no hyperacute changes associated with ischemic stroke. CT angiography shows no large vessel occlusion. What is the next best investigation in this clinical scenario?
questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia wakes with left-sided weakness affecting his face, arm, and leg, double vision, and profound ataxia. His wife quickly calls an ambulance and arrives at the emergency room one hour after waking from sleep. On further questioning, you determine his last known well time to be 10 p.m. the night prior (9 hours prior to the presentation). His NIHSS is 6. A non-contrast CT shows no intracranial hemorrhage and no hyperacute changes associated with ischemic stroke. CT angiography shows no large vessel occlusion. What is the next best investigation in this clinical scenario?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Brain MRI: The next best investigation to guide acute management in this case is a brain MRI. The patient's presentation of left-sided weakness affecting the face, arm, and leg, double vision, and profound ataxia suggests a possible posterior circulation stroke, involving the vertebrobasilar artery territory. CT imaging is less sensitive in detecting early ischemic changes in the posterior fossa compared to brain MRI, especially when performed within a short time window from symptom onset. Brain MRI, particularly with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequence, is highly sensitive and specific in detecting acute ischemic changes and can provide more detailed information about the location and extent of the stroke. It can also help rule out other potential etiologies, such as posterior fossa tumors or demyelinating disorders. Therefore, a brain MRI is the most appropriate next investigation to guide acute management in this patient. Incorrect Options: Option B - Carotid Duplex Ultrasonography: Carotid duplex ultrasonography is a non-invasive imaging technique used to assess the blood flow in the carotid arteries. While it is valuable in evaluating the carotid arteries for stenosis or occlusion in patients with suspected ischemic stroke, it may not be the most appropriate initial investigation in this case. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Right anterior inferior cerebellar artery : Infarction in the right anterior inferior cerebellar artery can result in acute sensorineural hearing loss. The classic syndrome associated with infarction of the anterior choroidal artery is one of contralateral hemiparesis, sensory loss, and a visual field deficit. The recurrent artery of Huebner is often the first branch off the anterior cerebral artery and occlusion can result in an isolated infarction of the caudate head. Occlusion of the right pericallosal artery can result in a frontal gyrus and/or corpus callosum infarct. The artery of Percheron is an anatomical variant resulting in a solitary paramedian thalamic branch and occlusion results in characteristic bilateral thalamic infarcts. questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding occipital nerve blocks in the management of headaches?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is true regarding occipital nerve blocks in the management of headaches?

options.label: A
options.text: Occipital nerve block is effective in approximately 30% of patients with occipital neuralgia

options.label: B
options.text: Ultrasound guidance is necessary for identification of the injection site

options.label: C
options.text: Aspiration before injection is paramount because the occipital artery runs lateral to the nerve

options.label: D
options.text: For most headache syndromes, the addition of steroids to the anesthetic increases the efficacy of the procedure with minimal added side effects

questions.answerText: Aspiration before injection is paramount because the occipital artery runs lateral to the nerve
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Aspiration before injection is paramount because the occipital artery runs lateral to the nerve: The occipital artery runs lateral to the nerve and palpation of its pulse can further help confirm the correct location. To avoid intravascular injection, aspiration before injection is extremely important (option C is correct). ONBs are usually performed using lidocaine and/or bupivacaine. Incorrect Options: Option A - Occipital nerve block is effective in approximately 30% of patients with occipital neuralgia: Occipital nerve blocks (ONBs) can be helpful both in the diagnosis and management of specific headache syndromes. The vast majority of patients with occipital neuralgia will respond to ONBs and response to ONBs is listed in the International Headache Society diagnostic criteria for the condition. Option B - Ultrasound guidance is necessary for identification of the injection site: Though ultrasound has been studied as a way to improve accuracy when performing ONBs, the use of ultrasound is not necessary for the procedure, which can be performed using anatomic landmarks in most patients. The ideal injection site is 2 cm lateral and 2 cm inferior to the external occipital protuberance in patients with otherwise normal cranial anatomy. Option D - For most headache syndromes, the addition of steroids to the anesthetic increases the efficacy of the procedure with minimal added side effects: For most headache syndromes, including migraine and occipital neuralgia, studies have failed to show improved outcomes by adding corticosteroids and injection of corticosteroids has been associated with increased risk of adverse reactions such as alopecia, and cutaneous atrophy with recurrent injections. Cluster headache constitutes a reasonable exception to this rule of avoiding corticosteroids with ONBs. @Neet_pg_bot

Your language exam is notable for impaired fluency and he appears to struggle a great deal in responding to your questions (both vocally and in writing). At one point you ask him about whether he has been compliant with his oral anti-coagulation and in his attempt to respond to your question he uses the term “coagulation.” He appears frustrated with the error and has no issues following written or spoken commands. Which of the following is true regarding the utility of testing repetition in this clinical context?

options.text: Preserved repetition would suggest a cortical sensory aphasia

options.label: B
options.text: Preserved repetition would suggest a transcortical sensory aphasia

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Preserved repetition would suggest a transcortical motor aphasia: This man is presenting with an ischemic stroke (until proven otherwise) with unclear time of onset and a motor aphasia. Motor aphasias, such as that of “Broca aphasia”, are defined by impaired fluency with intact comprehension. A classic way of remembering this has been that “Broca aphasia results in broken speech” as speech (as well as written communication) is often effortful and is missing bound morphemes (e.g., the fact that this patient missed “anti-“in his attempt to state the word “anticoagulation”). Broca (i.e., cortical motor aphasia) and transcortical motor aphasias have identical clinical features by observation and with additional bedside testing with a major distinguisher between the two being preserved repetition in the latter and impaired repetition in the former. Incorrect Options: Option A - Preserved repetition would suggest a cortical sensory aphasia: Cortical sensory aphasia, also known as Wernicke's aphasia, is characterized by fluent speech with impaired comprehension and meaningful yet nonsensical language. Repetition is typically impaired in individuals with Wernicke's aphasia. Option B - Preserved repetition would suggest a transcortical sensory aphasia: Transcortical sensory aphasia is a rare language disorder characterized by preserved repetition but impaired comprehension and fluent yet paraphasic speech. Individuals with transcortical sensory aphasia have difficulty understanding language, and their speech may be nonsensical or include words from other languages. Option C - Preserved repetition would suggest a cortical motor aphasia: Cortical motor aphasia, also known as Broca's aphasia, is characterized by non-fluent speech, limited vocabulary, and preserved comprehension. questions.stem: A 45-year-old blind patient seeks medical attention for long-standing sleep problems. He has been completely blind since age 32. For the past 10 years, he has suffered from periods of nocturnal insomnia and daytime sleepiness which are very disruptive to his work and family life. In between these periods of insomnia and daytime sleepiness, he may have weeks of near-normal night-time sleep. A 14-day actigraphy record shows a daily delay drift of the onset and offset of the sleep-wake rhythm with a circadian period that is longer than 24 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?

In between these periods of insomnia and daytime sleepiness, he may have weeks of near-normal night-time sleep. A 14-day actigraphy record shows a daily delay drift of the onset and offset of the sleep-wake rhythm with a circadian period that is longer than 24 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Non-24-hour sleep wake disorder: The scenario described is typical of non-24-hour sleep wake disorder (N24SWD), formerly known as free-running rhythm disorder, which is characterized by a chronic or recurrent pattern of sleep-wake cycles that are not entrained to the 24-hour environment. N24SWD predominantly affects blind individuals who have decreased light perception. Patients usually present with periods of insomnia and daytime sleepiness that alternate with periods when the patient is asymptomatic. Actigraphy shows a sleep-wake cycle that is not entrained to the 24-hour environment, typically with a daily drift to later and later times. Incorrect Options: Option A - Delayed sleep phase disorder: Delayed sleep phase disorder is caused by a delayed circadian rhythm and results in a tendency to stay up and wake up at times later than what is socially acceptable. Option B - Advanced sleep phase disorder: Advanced sleep-phase disorder is characterized by difficulty staying awake until a socially acceptable bedtime together with an earlier than desired wake-up time. Option C - Shift-work disorder: Patients with shift work disorder typically have excessive sleepiness during the wake (work) period and insomnia during the desired sleep period that occurs in association with an unconventional work schedule. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: You are attempting to better understand how genetic variations of various cytochrome P-450 enzymes affects oestrogen metabolism and ultimately impacts breast cancer incidence. You discover that this is due to a microsatellite variation with a 4 base pair sequence repetition within a P-450 enzyme gene. This is an example of what genetic principle?
questions.stemHtml: You are attempting to better understand how genetic variations of various cytochrome P-450 enzymes affects oestrogen metabolism and ultimately impacts breast cancer incidence. You discover that this is due to a microsatellite variation with a 4 base pair sequence repetition within a P-450 enzyme gene. This is an example of what genetic principle?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Genetic polymorphism: This example demonstrates a genetic polymorphism which results in a variant that affects oestrogen metabolism, ultimately putting the patient at a higher risk of developing breast cancer. In genetics, polymorphism is when multiple (more than 2) alleles can occupy a gene locus in the population. A polymorphic variant of a gene can be related to a disease, such as cancer. Genetic polymorphisms can occur due to a deletion or a duplication of a DNA base pair sequence. Both SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) and microsatellite variations are examples of polymorphisms. It is thought that genetic polymorphisms play a much larger role in cancer risk than high-penetrance mutations in tumour suppressor genes or oncogenes, which are more rare. Incorrect Options: Option A - Epigenetic silencing: Epigenetic silencing is a genetic term that refers to how a gene's expression is regulated. Typically, expression of a gene can be silenced by methylation or hypermethylation. There is published evidence of promoter CpG island hypermethylation driving the transcriptional repression of tumour-suppressor genes and ultimately leading to malignancy (Esteller., Hum Mol Genet 2007). Option C - Incomplete penetrance: Incomplete penetrance refers to a situation where not all individuals who carry a certain gene will express the symptom or trait associated with that gene. Option D - Genetic imprinting: Genetic imprinting, or genome imprinting, is when a gene expression varies depending on whether it was inherited from the father or the mother. There are ~75 examples that occur in humans. In medicine, an example of imprinting can be seen in Prader-Willi syndrome versus Angelman syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What hereditary condition is associated with an increased risk of developing desmoid tumours (aggressive fibromatosis)?
questions.stemHtml: What hereditary condition is associated with an increased risk of developing desmoid tumours (aggressive fibromatosis)?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Gardner Syndrome: Patients with Gardner syndrome are at risk of developing mesenteric fibromatosis (desmoid tumour). Gardner syndrome is a subtype of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP). It is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutation in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene located on chromosome 5. Patients are prone to developing multiple colon polyps, osteomas of the skull, fibromas, thyroid cancer, epidermoid cysts, and desmoid tumours. Desmoid tumours are rare and account for less than 5% of all soft tissue tumours, but ~5-15% of cases are associated with Gardner syndrome Incorrect Options: Option A - Cowden syndrome: Cowden syndrome, also called multiple hamartoma syndrome, is an autosomal dominant disorder marked by benign GI hamartomas as well as an increased risk of several malignancies (breast, thyroid, uterine, and others). Patients can also present with facial or periorificial trichilemmomas, perioral lentigines, cobble stoning of the oral mucosal surface, acral keratotic papules, fibromas, and lipomas Option C - Gorlin syndrome: Gorlin syndrome, also called nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome, is due to a mutation in the PTCH1 gene. PTCH1 is a tumour suppressor gene located on chromosome 9 that is part of the hedgehog signalling pathway. Most patients (≥ 90%) develop multiple basal cell carcinoma of the skin. Other signs and symptoms can include keratocystic odontogenic tumours, cardiac fibromas, ovarian fibromas, bone and skeletal abnormalities, and intracranial calcifications. Option D - Hyaline fibromatosis syndrome (HFS): Hyaline fibromatosis syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder that results in hyaline deposits in the skin and other tissue. It generally presents in infancy and can result in pain, joint contractures, thickened skin, and hyperpigmented patches overlying joints. @Neet_pg_bot

Her ECOG performance status is 0. Which of the following would you recommend as next step in management?

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Extra fascial hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO)
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Extra fascial hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO): The patient in the vignette above demonstrates complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. This process is secondary to thickening of the endometrial glands (typically due to unopposed oestrogen), and is considered a pre-cancerous lesion. Patients in this clinical situation that have completed childbearing should undergo a total extrafascial hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO). This recommendation is due to the relatively high probability of finding endometrial carcinoma during surgery. In addition, BSO is the standard of care in the treatment of endometrial carcinoma, and may spare the patient an additional surgical intervention. Incorrect Options: Option A - Extra Fascial Hysterectomy: While hysterectomy is a definitive treatment option, given the pathology result of complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypia, there is a potential for progression to endometrial cancer. Therefore, more comprehensive management might be considered. Option C - Medroxyprogesterone Acetate (MPA): Hormone therapy with MPA might be considered as a conservative approach to manage certain cases of complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. However, the patient's post-menopausal status and the potential for malignancy make surgical intervention a more appropriate choice. Option D - Observation: Given the diagnosis of complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypia, observation is generally not recommended. There is a potential for progression to endometrial cancer, and taking a more proactive approach to remove the source of the hyperplasia is often warranted. @Neet_pg_bot

Which of the following would you recommend for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Lurbinectedin: The current recommendation for patients relapsed within 6 months of treatment is Lurbinectedin. Lurbinectedin is an alkylating agent that is FDA approved for patients with metastatic small cell lung cancer (SCLC) with disease progression on or after platinum-based chemotherapy. This approval is based on a single-arm, open-label, phase 2 basket trial of patients with SCLC (no brain metastases) who progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy. With a median follow-up of 17.1 months they reported the following: Overall response rate (ORR) with lurbinectedin: 35.2% Median duration of response: was 5.3 months Patients still responding at 6 months: 43.0% Overall response rate (ORR) among patients with chemotherapy-free interval <90 days: 22% vs. 45% among patients with a chemotherapy-free interval ≥90 days 12 month overall survival among patients with chemotherapy-free interval <90 days: 12.9% vs. 48.3% among patients with a chemotherapy-free interval ≥90 days All patients in this study received a prespecified antiemetic regimen consisting of a corticosteroid and serotonin antagonist. Serious adverse reactions occurred in 10 percent of patients, of which neutropenia and febrile neutropenia were the most common (5 percent for each). Incorrect Options: Option A - Paclitaxel: Paclitaxel is a chemotherapy drug commonly used in the treatment of various cancers, including lung cancer. However, it is not a standard treatment option for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (SCLC) as a single agent. The standard chemotherapy regimen for extensive-stage SCLC typically includes a combination of cisplatin or carboplatin with etoposide. Option B - Doxorubicin: Doxorubicin is another chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of various cancers. While it has shown activity against some solid tumour’s, including lung cancer, it is not commonly used as a standard treatment for extensive-stage SCLC. Option C - Vinblastine: Vinblastine is a chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of certain cancers, but it is not a standard treatment option for extensive-stage SCLC. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Degarelix: This patient presents with extensive epidural extension of tumor in the spinal canal and an impending spinal cord compression. Degarelix is a gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonist that inhibits GnRH receptors in the pituitary gland. Unlike GnRH agonists, this will NOT produce an initial surge in luteinizing hormone. Buserelin, goserelin, leuprolide, and triptorelin are all GnRH agonists that will continually activate the receptor and ultimately result in decreased levels of gonadotropins (luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone) and decreased testosterone production from the testis. However, because these drugs are receptor agonists, they may initially result in a luteinizing hormone surge and transient serum testosterone increase. This transient increase in testosterone could result in a strong stimulus for tumor growth, and should be avoided in cases where there may be significant toxicity from tumor progression (such as impending spinal cord or cauda equina compression or impending bladder outlet obstruction). While it's a valid option, there are other agents that are often preferred due to their efficacy and side effect profiles. Option C - Goserelin: Goserelin is another LHRH agonist used in ADT for prostate cancer. Like Buserelin, it's a valid option, but GnRH antagonists like Degarelix have gained popularity for their more rapid onset of action. Option D - Leuprolide: Leuprolide is also a common LHRH agonist used in ADT for prostate cancer. It's effective at reducing testosterone levels over time but might not offer the same rapid suppression as GnRH antagonists like Degarelix. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Bone scan: Adenocarcinomas are not typically associated with primary bone involvement. Instead, they are more commonly associated with primary sites in organs such as the lung, breast, colon, or prostate. Therefore, the presence of a large mediastinal mass in this case suggests a primary malignancy in the mediastinum itself rather than metastatic bone involvement. The decision to perform a bone scan should be based on clinical indications and the type of tumor. In this case, a testicular ultrasound is more relevant due to the possibility of primary mediastinal germ cell tumors, which can have a testicular origin. Meropenem, amikacin, and tigecycline (for antibiotic-resistant Enterobacter) are ordered. A stress dose of steroids is started. A central line and an arterial line are placed. questions.stem: The immune response of lipopolysaccharides triggering hypotension is exercised by the immune system through which of the following receptors?
questions.stemHtml: The immune response of lipopolysaccharides triggering hypotension is exercised by the immune system through which of the following receptors?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Toll Like Receptor (TLR): LPS is a building block of the wall among gram-negative bacteria. This is a highly immunogenic compound that is recognized by a special group of toll-like receptor. LPS is recognized by TLR type 4. A series of clinical trials has been aimed at the TLR-related pathway in an effort to control the inflammatory response during sepsis. Activation of the TLR receptor triggers non-specific innate immunity. Hypotension ensues due to the release of several vasoactive components. Incorrect Options: Option B - Β-adrenergic receptor: The β-adrenergic receptors are primarily involved in the regulation of the sympathetic nervous system, specifically the fight-or-flight response. These receptors are mainly activated by catecholamines like epinephrine and norepinephrine. While β-adrenergic receptors play a crucial role in cardiovascular regulation, they are not directly involved in the immune response triggered by lipopolysaccharides (LPS) and do not mediate the hypotension associated with septic shock. Option C - α-adrenergic receptor: The α-adrenergic receptors are another class of adrenergic receptors that are also involved in the regulation of the sympathetic nervous system. They are primarily activated by norepinephrine and play a role in vascular smooth muscle contraction, leading to vasoconstriction and an increase in blood pressure. While α-adrenergic receptors are involved in cardiovascular regulation, they are not responsible for the immune response triggered by LPS in septic shock. Option D - PF4 receptor: PF4 (Platelet Factor 4) is a molecule released from platelets upon activation. While it does have some immunomodulatory effects and acts as a chemoattractant, it is not directly involved in the immune response triggered by LPS. Additionally, the PF4 receptor is not specifically known for its role in septic shock or the hypotension associated with it. PF4 is more commonly associated with platelet activation and plays a role in conditions like heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which bacterial infection is most commonly associated with Guillain-Barre syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: Which bacterial infection is most commonly associated with Guillain-Barre syndrome?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Campylobacter jejuni: Approximately 66% of patients with Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) had a preceding infection, surgery, or vaccination within the month prior to the onset of symptoms. Campylobacter jejuni is the most common bacterial infection associated with GBS. Estimates vary, as C. jejuni is found in 17-42% of patients with GBS. It is specifically associated with the axonal variant, acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN). C. jejuni infections are evident in up to 76% of these patients. Mycoplasma pneumonia is often seen in children with GBS. GBS has also been linked to Hemophilus influenzae. Viral infections associated with GBS include cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, varicella-zoster, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and HIV. Isolated cases have been associated with vaccinations (e.g. influenza, tetanus, diphtheria, rabies, oral polio) and drugs (e.g. heroin, streptokinase). The risk of GBS with influenza vaccination is approximately 1:1,000,000. Incorrect Options: Option A - Staphylococcus aureus: Staphylococcus aureus is a common bacterial pathogen, but it is not commonly associated with Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS). GBS is primarily linked to infections with Campylobacter jejuni, not Staphylococcus aureus. Option B - Streptococcus pneumoniae: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a bacterial pathogen responsible for causing various infections, including pneumonia, sinusitis, and meningitis. While bacterial infections can sometimes precede GBS, Streptococcus pneumoniae is not the most commonly associated pathogen with GBS. Campylobacter jejuni is the bacteria most commonly linked to GBS. Option C - Enterococci: Enterococci are a group of bacteria that can cause infections, particularly in healthcare settings. However, they are not commonly associated with Guillain-Barre syndrome. The primary bacterial association with GBS is Campylobacter jejuni. @Neet_pg_bot

Incorrect Options: Option A - Start oseltamivir and go to work: Starting oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is a reasonable step if you suspect you have influenza, as it is an antiviral medication that can help reduce the severity and duration of symptoms if taken early in the course of the illness. However, going to work while experiencing influenza-like symptoms is not recommended, as influenza is highly contagious, and you could easily spread the virus to your coworkers. Going to work in this condition would not only put your colleagues at risk of getting sick but could also worsen your own condition and delay your recovery. Option C - Do not start medication and go to work: Choosing not to start oseltamivir and still going to work while experiencing symptoms of influenza is not advisable. Influenza is a contagious respiratory illness that can spread easily from person to person, especially in close settings like workplaces. By not taking antiviral medication, you are not addressing the underlying cause of your symptoms, and you risk exposing your coworkers to the virus, which could lead to a workplace outbreak. Option D - Go to work and wear a face mask: Wearing a face mask may provide some level of protection to others if you have influenza, as it can help contain respiratory droplets that may carry the virus. However, it is not a substitute for staying home when you are sick. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Thymoma: Thymoma is the most likely diagnosis in this case. Thymomas are tumors that arise from the thymus gland in the anterior mediastinum. They can often be detected on a chest X-ray as a mass. The "thymic sail sign" refers to the appearance of the thymoma abutting the superior vena cava (SVC) and resembling the sail of a boat. Thymomas are typically slow-growing and may be asymptomatic or present with symptoms related to compression of nearby structures. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hodgkin's lymphoma: Hodgkin's lymphoma typically presents with enlarged lymph nodes, often in the neck, armpit, or groin. Option C - Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism is a condition where a blood clot travels to the lungs, causing sudden symptoms like shortness of breath, chest pain, and rapid heart rate. Option D - Aortic aneurysm: An aortic aneurysm involves the dilation of the aorta, the main blood vessel leaving the heart.
