questions.stem: A 55-year-old patient presents with a history of fatigue, and bone pains. He has had a history of hypertension and diabetes for the past 20 years. He was diagnosed with chronic renal failure, 2 years ago. His complete blood count and basic metabolic profile are ordered. On lab results, his calcium is low, PTH is high and phosphate is high. What should be the next possible treatment for this patient addressing the bone pains?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old patient presents with a history of fatigue, and bone pains. He has had a history of hypertension and diabetes for the past 20 years. He was diagnosed with chronic renal failure, 2 years ago. His complete blood count and basic metabolic profile are ordered. On lab results, his calcium is low, PTH is high and phosphate is high. What should be the next possible treatment for this patient addressing the bone pains?

options.label: D
options.text: Phosphate binders and low phosphorus diet

questions.answerText: Phosphate binders and low phosphorus diet
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Phosphate binders and low phosphorus diet: Renal bone disease is a condition that occurs due to chronic kidney disease (CKD), where the kidneys cannot maintain the proper balance of calcium and phosphorus in the body. This imbalance can lead to a variety of bone-related problems, including: Osteomalacia: a condition where the bones become weak due to a lack of vitamin D. In chronic renal failure, 25-OH Vitamin D cannot be converted to 1,25-OH Vitamin D and hence the deficiency of calcium. Secondary hyperparathyroidism: the parathyroid gland becomes overactive due to a lack of calcium and due to increased phosphate levels (which stimulate the production of fibroblast growth factor 23), leading to increased PTH levels. Increased osteoclastic bone resorption: due to lack of bone mineralisation (deficiency of vitamin D) and also due to increased PTH levels. Treatment for renal bone disease typically involves a combination of medications and dietary changes to help manage the imbalance of calcium and phosphorus levels in the body, as well as manage the underlying kidney disease. Phosphate binders (e.g calcium carbonate, sevelamer, etc) may be prescribed to help control phosphorus levels. A diet rich in high phosphorus levels should be restricted too. Active Vitamin D supplements may also be used to address hypocalcemia. In some cases with persistent hyperparathyroidism, parathyroidectomy or medications such as cinacalcet may be used to help control PTH levels. Incorrect Options: Option A - Emergency Parathyroidectomy: Parathyroidectomy is only done if there is persistent hyperparathyroidism despite the dietary changes or medications. It is not the first line step in the management of renal bone disease. Option B - Cinacalcet : Cinacalcet is a drug that reduces PTH secretion. It is used if parathyroidectomy is unsuccessful or it cannot be done in some instances. Option C - Increased sun exposure : Increased sun exposure is not an appropriate treatment for the patient's condition. Sun exposure is a source of vitamin D, however, vitamin D is not converted to its active form in a patient with chronic renal failure. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with edema, fatigue, and frothy urine. Blood tests show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Urinalysis shows proteinuria, with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 5. A kidney biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and spike-like projections on silver stain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old female presents with edema, fatigue, and frothy urine. Blood tests show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Urinalysis shows proteinuria, with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 5. A kidney biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and spike-like projections on silver stain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Membranous nephropathy: Membranous nephropathy is a type of glomerulonephritis that affects the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) of the kidneys, leading to proteinuria and often nephrotic syndrome. It is a relatively common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, with an estimated incidence of 2-10 cases per million per year. The diagnosis of membranous nephropathy is typically made based on a combination of clinical presentation, laboratory tests, and kidney biopsy findings. The clinical presentation usually includes edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia. Urine tests will show significant proteinuria, often with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of greater than 3-4. Blood tests may show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Kidney biopsy is necessary to confirm the diagnosis of membranous nephropathy and to distinguish it from other types of glomerulonephritis. The biopsy findings in membranous nephropathy typically show diffuse thickening of the GBM, with subepithelial immune complex deposits that can be seen on electron microscopy. questions.solution: Correct Option B: Accumulation of organic acids Kidneys are the vital organs of the human body that play an important role in the filtration of blood and excretion of metabolic wastes. Kidneys also produce important hormones like vitamin D, erythropoietin, etc. This patient is suffering from metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap. This metabolic acidosis results from the accumulation of organic acids in the body. Some of the causes of renal failure are diabetes, high blood pressure, chronic NSAID users, etc. The accumulation of organic acids is the main reason for the increased anion gap. Some of the symptoms of kidney failure are decreased urine output, fatigue, muscle cramps, fluid overload, nausea, vomiting, dry skin, etc. Incorrect options: Option A: Ketones accumulation Ketone accumulation can also result in an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis but in renal failure, the main cause of metabolic acidosis is the accumulation of organic acids. Ketones are accumulated in the body in diabetes. It is a common condition in type I diabetes mellitus in which insulin is deficient. The salicylate overdose can result in metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap but in renal failure, the main cause of metabolic acidosis is the accumulation of organic acids. It can also cause respiratory alkalosis initially because of the increased respiratory drive. questions.solution: Correct Option B: Type 2 Renal tubular acidosis In Fanconi syndrome, there is a defect in the proximal tubule function including reabsorption. Fanconi syndrome can be inherited or acquired. Due to defects in reabsorption, glucose, protein, phosphate along other substances appear in the urine. Patients with Fanconi syndrome also have defective reabsorption of bicarbonate which results in type 2 renal tubular acidosis with hypokalemia and normal anion gap. Even in the presence of glucosuria, blood glucose level remains in the normal range. Also, proteinuria is mild and not clinically significant. Incorrect options: Option A: Type 1 renal tubular acidosis In type 1 renal tubular acidosis, there is a defect in the Excretion of hydrogen ions from the distal tubule by the kidney. Type 1 RTA results in muscle weakness, constipation, irregular heart rate, paralysis and death. Urine pH in type 1 RTA is > 5.5 and also no cast, RBCs, glucose and protein in the urine. Option C: Type 4 renal tubular acidosis In type 4 RTA, there is either a decreased circulating level of aldosterone or aldosterone resistance. Causes include Addison’s disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, ACEIs, ARBs, and pseudohypoaldosteronism. Type 4 RTA, there is acidosis, salt wasting and hyperkalemia. Option D: Diabetic ketoacidosis In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), there is a high blood glucose level with elevated blood ketone level. Symptoms of DKA include anorexia, vomiting, abdominal pain, polyuria, polydipsia, and a fruity odor to breathe (Kassmaul breathing). ABGs show acidemia, with a high anion gap. Urine analysis shows glucose and ketones but mild or no protein in the urine. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C: Decreased excretion of hydrogen ions from distal tubule of the nephron. Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule of the nephron. Aldosterone causes increased sodium reabsorption and increased Excretion of hydrogen ions and potassium. Deficiency of aldosterone leads to decreased reabsorption of sodium, and decreased Excretion of hydrogen ions and potassium leading to salt wasting, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis. Etiology of hypoaldosteronism includes autoimmune hypoaldosteronism, T.B. involving the adrenal gland, adrenal hemorrhage, ACEIs, ARBs, and pseudohypoaldosteronism. Symptoms of weakness, fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, hypoglycemia, ( due to decreased cortisol), hypotension, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis (decreased Aldosterone) and hyperpigmentation (increased ACTH). Decreased reabsorption of bicarbonate from the proximal convoluted tubule leads to metabolic acidosis but in this patient, metabolic acidosis is due to a deficiency of Aldosterone which acts on the distal tubule, not on the proximal convoluted tubule. Option B: Increased reabsorption of bicarbonate from the lumen of the distal tubule of the nephron. Aldosterone action on the distal tubule is to reabsorb sodium and excrete hydrogen ions and potassium. Aldosterone does not directly reabsorb bicarbonate from the lumen of the distal tubule. It indirectly helps in the reabsorption of bicarbonate into circulation that is formed inside cells of the distal tubule. As in this case, there is a deficiency of Aldosterone, there will be decreased reabsorption of bicarbonate. Option D: Increased Excretion of hydrogen ions from the loop of Henle. Aldosterone action is on the distal tubule of the nephron. Aldosterone has no action on the loop of Henle. Function of the loop of Henle is to reabsorb electrolytes. It has no role in acid-base balance. @Neet_pg_bot

Defective beta chains in hemoglobin make RBCs susceptible to sickling in the condition of hypoxia, dehydration and acidosis. Sickled RBCs are irregular in shape and stuck in small blood vessels resulting in vaso-occlusive crisis and hemolysis. Symptoms of sickle cell disease include pallor, jaundice, episodes of pain, swelling of hands and feet, recurrent infections, growth retardation, vision the problem, auto splenectomy (due to infarction). Sickle cell disease is also one of the causes of renal tubular acidosis type 1. Peripheral smear shows target cells and sickled RBCs. questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Labs reveal blood glucose of 460 mg/dL, pH of 7.20, and potassium of 2.2 mEq/L. Urinalysis is positive for ketones. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Labs reveal blood glucose of 460 mg/dL, pH of 7.20, and potassium of 2.2 mEq/L. Urinalysis is positive for ketones. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.solution: Correct Option A. Administer 0.45% NaCl infusion: This is the correct initial intervention. The patient is presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which is characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. The low blood pH (7.20) indicates acidosis. The patient's low potassium level (2.2 mEq/L) suggests hypokalemia, likely due to intracellular shifts of potassium as a result of acidosis. Administering a 0.45% NaCl (normal saline) infusion helps to correct dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and acidosis. It also assists in improving tissue perfusion. After initiating fluid resuscitation, insulin administration can be started to help lower blood glucose levels and further correct acidosis Incorrect options: Option B. Administer potassium chloride: While hypokalemia (low potassium) is a potential complication of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), administering potassium chloride as the initial intervention can be dangerous. The patient's potassium level is already low (2.2 mEq/L), and administering potassium without proper fluid resuscitation can lead to further imbalances and potentially life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Correcting fluid balance is the priority before addressing potassium imbalances. Option C. Administer 0.1 units/kg IV insulin: While insulin administration is a crucial component of DKA treatment, it should not be the initial step in this case. Before insulin is administered, it's important to address the patient's fluid and electrolyte imbalances. Administering insulin without adequate hydration can lead to further decreases in potassium levels and potential complications. Option D. Administer a dextrose solution: Administering a dextrose solution is not appropriate as the initial intervention for DKA. The patient's blood glucose level is already very high (460 mg/dL), and giving more glucose can exacerbate the hyperglycemia and worsen the acidosis. The primary concern in DKA management is first addressing fluid and electrolyte imbalances. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male presents with a headache, nausea, vomiting, and dizziness after climbing to an altitude of 12,000 feet. Physical examination reveals an unsteady gait, and the patient is diagnosed with mountain sickness. Which of the following diuretics is most useful in the management of mountain sickness?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male presents with a headache, nausea, vomiting, and dizziness after climbing to an altitude of 12,000 feet. Physical examination reveals an unsteady gait, and the patient is diagnosed with mountain sickness. Which of the following diuretics is most useful in the management of mountain sickness?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Acetazolamide Acetazolamide is a diuretic that primarily acts in the proximal tubules of the kidney to inhibit the enzyme carbonic anhydrase . Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the reversible reaction between water and carbon dioxide to form bicarbonate and a hydrogen ion . Inhibition of this enzyme by acetazolamide leads to decreased bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubules , which in turn leads to increased excretion of bicarbonate and a reduction in the reabsorption of sodium and water . As a result, the body attempts to compensate for this by increasing respiratory rate, heart rate and by increasing bicarbonate reabsorption in the kidneys. questions.solution: Correct Option A: Lisinopril Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor medication that is commonly used in the treatment of CKD. It acts by blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. By inhibiting angiotensin II, lisinopril reduces aldosterone secretion and promotes sodium and water excretion, which can lead to hyperkalemia. Angiotensin II specifically constrict the efferent arteriole and increases the glomerular filtration pressure, and increases the proteinuria. One of the therapeutic effects of ACE inhibitors is reducing proteinuria by dilating the efferent arteriole and thus decreasing the filtration pressure, which ultimately leads to reduced proteinuria, which is a common complication of CKD. It decreases sodium reabsorption and therefore decreases fluid reabsorption; this directly causes decreased levels of circulating sodium. It does not have a significant effect on reducing proteinuria. questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and hypertension presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath, confusion, and lethargy. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals a pH of 7.40, pCO2 of 60 mmHg, and HCO3- of 28 mEq/L. Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for the patient's acid-base disturbance?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Furosemide Furosemide is a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na+/K+/2Cl- co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, leading to increased excretion of sodium, chloride, and water. Furosemide can also cause metabolic alkalosis due to volume depletion, chloride depletion, and potassium wasting. The loss of chloride ions can cause bicarbonate ions to accumulate in the extracellular fluid, leading to an increase in pH. However, in this case, the patient has developed respiratory acidosis due to the retention of carbon dioxide, possibly due to decreased respiratory drive caused by the confusion and lethargy. The combination of respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis has resulted in a compensated acid-base disturbance, as evidenced by the near-normal HCO3- level. Incorrect options: Option A: Aspirin Aspirin can cause metabolic acidosis by increasing the production of lactic acid and impairing renal acid excretion, but this is not the likely cause of the patient's acid-base disturbance. Option B: Amoxicillin Amoxicillin is an antibiotic that does not typically cause acid-base disturbances . Option D: Metformin Metformin is an antidiabetic medication that can cause lactic acidosis, but this is a rare side effect and is not the likely cause of the patient's acid-base disturbance. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A: pH - 7.28 Anion gap - 18 pCO2 (mm Hg) - 29 Bicarbonate (mEq/L) - 15 This patient, who presents with an altered mental status and an elevated blood urea nitrogen level after missed hemodialysis, is most likely suffering from uremia leading to metabolic acidosis. A low pH and bicarbonate level with an increased anion gap is consistent with an anion gap metabolic acidosis, which occurs in end-stage renal disease (ESRD) due to a build-up of certain acidic anions (e.g., phosphate, sulfate, hippurate, urate). Metabolic acidosis increases respiratory drive (respiratory compensation), resulting in a decrease in arterial pCO2 that the Winter formula can predict. If the patient's measured pCO2 falls outside the expected pCO2, a secondary respiratory acid-base disorder (e.g., respiratory acidosis due to uremic encephalopathy and CNS depression, respiratory alkalosis due to ESRD-induced pulmonary oedema) should be considered. Incorrect Options: Option B: pH - 7.49 Anion gap - 10 pCO2 (mm Hg) - 25 Bicarbonate (mEq/L) - 28 This statement is incorrect as elevated pH and decreased pCO2 levels are consistent with respiratory alkalosis without metabolic compensation (normal bicarbonate ), which occurs due to increased respiratory rate and tidal volume (i.e. alveolar hyperventilation). This patient has no signs of hyperventilation or increased tidal volumes. Instead, he has uremia, which puts him at risk of developing a different acid-base disorder. The increased serum pH decreases respiratory drive (respiratory compensation), resulting in an increased arterial pCO2. Instead, this patient has uremia, which puts him at risk of a different acid-base disorder. Despite aggressive medical management, including intracranial pressure monitoring and therapies to reduce cerebral edema, the patient's neurological status continues to deteriorate. options.label: B

options.label: D

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Absence of all brainstem reflexes: Brain death is a clinical diagnosis made when there is evidence of irreversible cessation of all cerebral and brainstem activities. To determine brain death, the following clinical criteria are typically considered: Absence of all brainstem reflexes, including: Pupillary reflex (pupils fixed and dilated) Corneal reflex Oculocephalic reflex (doll's eye reflex) Oculovestibular reflex (absent caloric responses) Facial motor responses (absent facial movements) Absence of all cerebral functions, including: No evidence of motor responses to painful stimuli Absence of spontaneous breathing (apnea) It's essential to emphasize that brain death is a clinical diagnosis, and confirmatory tests, such as cerebral blood flow studies or electroencephalography (EEG), may be used to support the clinical findings. Incorrect Options: Option B - Absence of cranial nerve II (optic nerve) function: While cranial nerve II (optic nerve) function may be impaired in patients with severe brain injury, it is not a crucial component in the determination of brain death. Brain death is primarily based on the absence of brainstem reflexes and cerebral functions. Option C - Persistent vegetative state with minimal responsiveness: A persistent vegetative state is a different clinical condition characterized by preserved brainstem function but a lack of higher cortical function and awareness. It is distinct from brain death. Option D - Non-reactive pupils in response to light: While non-reactive pupils can be indicative of brain dysfunction, they are not sufficient on their own to confirm brain death. Brain death diagnosis requires the absence of all brainstem reflexes, not just pupil reactivity. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Immediate transfer to the ER: This is a pit viper bite with envenomation . Copperheads and sometimes rattlesnakes are found in wood piles. When a crotalid viper envenomates (which is only 20-25% of the time), the initial wound may appear subtle, however, over several hours it will swell and show hemorrhage and eschar . Untreated, significant systemic coagulopathy can develop along with tissue necrosis. He needs immediate ER transfer for evaluation and consideration of crotalid antivenom . Brown recluse spiders also live in wood piles and their bites result in local effects, tissue necrosis, and occasional systemic effects. The effects of recluse spider envenomation do not progress this rapidly and envenomation is not associated with hemorrhage. It is important to recognize snake envenomation so it can be treated rapidly before progression. Incorrect Options: Option A - Soak it in betadine and open up the eschar: Soak it in betadine and open up the eschar: Opening up the eschar or attempting to manipulate the wound in this manner can potentially worsen the injury, introduce infection, and increase the risk of complications. Immediate transfer to the ER is the priority for proper evaluation and management of pit viper envenomation. questions.stem: A 23-year-old military recruit presents to the emergency department four days after a boot camp. He has been exercising vigorously in the heat, in uniform, and he has developed a rash on his neck, trunk, and thighs, which have been covered during his time out of doors. He notes he has been sweating heavily since he is not used to the heat. The rash is characterized by erythematous 2 to 4 mm papular and papulovesicular lesions. Which of the following is the first-line treatment for this patient's most likely diagnosis?

He has been exercising vigorously in the heat, in uniform, and he has developed a rash on his neck, trunk, and thighs, which have been covered during his time out of doors. He notes he has been sweating heavily since he is not used to the heat. The rash is characterized by erythematous 2 to 4 mm papular and papulovesicular lesions. Which of the following is the first-line treatment for this patient's most likely diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.text: Remove to cool environment and use topical antibiotics

questions.answerText: Remove to cool environment and use topical antibiotics
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Remove to cool environment and use topical antibiotics: Miliaria rubra (prickly heat) is an acute inflammatory disorder of the skin that occurs in tropical climates, as the result of blockage of the duct, usually within the epidermis , although it can occur in the dermis. Leakage of sweat causes inflammation in the periductal tissue. Miliaria rubra is characterized by erythematous 2 to 4 mm papules. They may be papulovesicular or pustular, and background erythema is often seen. Move patient to a cooler environment, if possible Wear breathable clothing (such as cotton) that does not occlude the skin Remove occlusive bandages in the affected area and use more porous alternatives, if needed Treat fever with antipyretics In addition, daily gentle exfoliation with a rough cloth during bathing or showering may help to improve milaria by removing debris (eg, corneocytes, sebum, etc) that may occlude the eccrine duct. The use of soap in patients with milaria rubra is controversial because of the potential for inducing additional skin irritation. In our experience, soap is helpful if not combined with aggressive scrubbing. Incorrect Options: Option A - Salicylic acid, 1%: Salicylic acid, 1%, can be applied three times daily to localized areas, but should not be used over large areas due to intoxication. For diffuse rashes, erythromycin can be helpful. Routine use of talcum or baby powder should be avoided. Option B - Oral antibiotics : Oral antibiotics are not indicated. Option C - Baby powder : Talcum should not be used. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 23-year-old male skater is found after an avalanche in Shimla. He was buried under the snow for 5 minutes and it took his friends 3 hours to carry him to the base of the mountain. On exam, his fingers of the left hand are blistered and cold. What temperature is ideal for thawing frozen extremities?
questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old male skater is found after an avalanche in Shimla. He was buried under the snow for 5 minutes and it took his friends 3 hours to carry him to the base of the mountain. On exam, his fingers of the left hand are blistered and cold. What temperature is ideal for thawing frozen extremities?
questions.solution: Correct answer: B - 37-39°C. Frostbitten tissue should be rapidly rewarmed in circulating water maintained at 37–39°C when refreezing can be prevented. The water temperature must be monitored to avoid thermal injury. Treat significant hypothermia and other life-threatening injuries first.

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Garlic – Arsenic: Garlic odor is associated with certain toxic substances, including arsenic compounds. Physical exam is concerning for ataxia and speech changes. Which of the following statements is consistent with therapy for this patient's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Recompression therapy can be initiated up to 3 weeks later

options.label: B
options.text: In-water recompression is the most effective method

options.label: C
options.text: Minor symptoms do not require treatment

questions.solution: Correct Option D - All patients should be recompressed: Arterial gas embolism (AGE) typically results when air bubbles are forced across the alveolar-capillary membrane, escape into the pulmonary venous circulation, and proceed through the left atrium and ventricle into the arterial circulation. The most common presentation of AGE includes global alteration of consciousness, headache, dizziness, convulsions, and visual changes. Although spontaneous resolution of symptoms may occur, all patients should be recompressed. Incorrect Options: Option A - Recompression therapy can be initiated up to 3 weeks later : Recompression therapy for decompression sickness may be initiated as late as 10-14 days after exposure. Option B - In-water recompression is the most effective method: In-water recompression is risky, demanding, time-consuming, and not typically recommended. Option C - Minor symptoms do not require treatment : Minor symptoms may progress, and the relapse rate is high in untreated cases. @Neet_pg_bot

The other fingers and toes are tender to touch and very cold. What is your immediate treatment for the patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Apply warm, wet towels to the extremities and cover him with a Bair Hugger warming device

options.label: B
options.text: Immerse his numb fingers and toes in a water bath warmed to 104 degrees. Wrap him in a warm blanket

options.label: C
options.text: Turn the heat in the patient's room up to 80 degrees and elevate his extremities

options.label: D
options.text: Infuse saline warmed to 100 degrees and cover him with a warm blanket

questions.answerText: Immerse his numb fingers and toes in a water bath warmed to 104 degrees. Wrap him in a warm blanket
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Immerse his numb fingers and toes in a water bath warmed to 104 degrees. Wrap him in a warm blanket: The patient has frostbite on two extremities. In frostbite, crystals form in the subcutaneous tissues and must be warmed as quickly as possible to minimize permanent damage. The ideal way to do this is to immerse the affected area in warm water to about 104 degrees , keeping the tissue off the edge of the basin. This patient is only mildly hypothermic and only needs a warm blanket while you address his frostbite. Although at some point the patient may need labs and a tox screen, this is of secondary concern given his frostbite. Incorrect Options: Option A - Apply warm, wet towels to the extremities and cover him with a Bair Hugger warming device: Rewarming is secondary in consideration to this patient's frostbite injury, although passive external rewarming is the treatment indicated for mild hypothermia. Option C - Turn the heat in the patient's room up to 80 degrees and elevate his extremities: Turning the heat up in the room and elevating the patient's extremities is not a treatment for hypothermia. Option D - Infuse saline warmed to 100 degrees and cover him with a warm blanket: Infusion of saline is an aggressive strategy of active internal rewarming generally reserved for patients with moderate hypothermia who do not respond to less aggressive measures, or for patients with severe hypothermia. @Neet_pg_bot
